title: The Un-Ordered UN Order
gist: Teaser: Mark Leonard argues the international order is in its worst shape since 1945 as the UN General Assembly meets, with China and Russia rejecting it, middle powers resenting it and the US public no longer willing to fund it; the new environment rewards improvisers over rule-makers, which Europe must adapt to.

insights.claim: The international order is in worse shape than at any point since 1945, as the 81st UN General Assembly convenes.
insights.speaker: @markhleonard
insights.so_what: Weaker multilateral guardrails raise baseline geopolitical risk premia.
insights.quote: the international order they have ostensibly come to defend is in worse shape than at any point since 1945

insights.claim: The post-Cold War system is losing support on three fronts: China and Russia never fully accepted it, newly assertive middle powers resent it, and its principal financial backer, the American public, has lost interest in underwriting it.
insights.speaker: @markhleonard
insights.so_what: Loss of the US as funder implies funding gaps and reduced capacity of multilateral institutions.
insights.quote: its principal financial backer, the American public, has lost interest in underwriting it

insights.claim: With the UN about to choose a new secretary-general and the Trump administration openly hostile to multilateralism, it is unclear how much longer the UN system can stagger on.
insights.speaker: @markhleonard
insights.so_what: UN leadership transition is a watchpoint for further institutional decline.
insights.quote: it is unclear how much longer the system can stagger on

insights.claim: The old world belonged to rule-makers and institution-builders, whereas the current landscape favors those who can improvise, so European leaders must adopt new, more flexible forms of multilateralism.
insights.speaker: @markhleonard
insights.so_what: Expect ad hoc coalitions and deal-by-deal diplomacy rather than durable treaties, raising policy volatility.
insights.quote: The old world belonged to rule-makers and institution-builders, but the current one favors those who can improvise.
